records.name: Belarus
records.current_summary:
Belarus is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In 2024 the authorities escalated from hostility to active persecution: a Culture Ministry decree reclassified transgender identity itself — "the desire to live and be seen by others as a person of an opposite sex" — as pornography, punishable by up to four years in prison. In September 2024 a wave of arrests targeted the community: TG House Belarus documented over 15 LGBTQ+ people detained, including at least eight transgender people, several arrested for merely subscribing to "extremist" resources online.

Detained trans people were beaten and forced to record humiliating "confession videos" circulated on pro-government channels. ODIHR's 2024 reporting notes the majority of bias incidents in Belarus targeted trans people, including "physical assaults, threats, abductions, humiliation, and coerced confessions related to their gender identity by law enforcement officers." State media runs systematic dehumanising propaganda.

Gender transition technically remains legal, but the 2024 pornography decree means a discoverable online presence or simply living visibly as trans can be prosecuted. For a visitor: no documented trans-tourist case yet, but police actively hunt trans people, any visible gender nonconformity risks detention, and foreign nationals receive no protection.
records.current_localsOnly: Gender transition technically remains legal for residents, but the 2024 pornography decree criminalises living visibly as trans — the decree's prosecution machinery targets residents' daily lives.
records.current_outOfScope: General political repression and the post-2020 protest crackdown affect everyone; the score reflects trans-specific risk.

sources.claim: HRW (12 Apr 2024): Belarusian law redefines 'pornography' to include depictions of same-sex relationships and transgender people, classed with necrophilia/paedophilia as 'non-traditional relationships'; production punishable by up to 4 years (13 for child material). Explicitly aimed at LGBT dignity — a persecution vector for visitors and residents alike.

JURIST (28 Sep 2024): TG House Belarus reports 15+ LGBTQ people detained in one month, incl. 8 transgender — most charged with hooliganism, two with pornography; custody abuse (physical and psychological) reported and some fled the country.

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Belarus: Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since 2015 and has no National Point of Contact; civil-society reports for 2024 came from Human Constanta and others. No official data available.
AP: 'Activists say police in Belarus beat LGBTQ+ people while arresting and charging them' — rights groups report beatings, coerced charges and expanding 'LGBT propaganda' repression.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Belarus: state TV equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and called them 'a weapon in the hands of the West'; TG House recorded increased hate speech in state propaganda; the Prosecutor General's Office plans an administrative-penalty law against 'LGBTI propaganda' (not yet tabled); at least ten trans people left Belarus in a year due to discrimination and repression; a new National Security Concept emphasises 'traditional values'.

ILGA World Treaty Bodies Strategic Litigation Toolkit, Part 2 - Case Digest (2024): compilation of UN Treaty Body decisions on 25 SOGIESC cases (criminalisation, asylum, violence, expression, families, legal gender recognition) - includes jurisprudence relevant to Belarus among other states.

US State Department 1999 Human Rights Report for Belarus (archived): historical baseline - documents the legal and social situation including treatment of homosexuality under the Lukashenka government.

Report 'Are all equal before the law?' (Bortnik & Sementsov, citing Amnesty International 2006-2007 context): Belarus's constitutional equality guarantee (Article 22) versus reality - clampdown on civil society, harassment of activists, arbitrary detentions, death penalty retained; the legal and political climate facing LGBT people in Belarus.

freshness_all.fact: April 2026 law criminalises 'propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness' — a new enforcement layer post-dating every cited 2024-25 source; acts remain legal, zero protections.

records.name: Ukraine
records.current_summary:
Ukraine is workable for trans visitors, with the caveat that this scores trans-specific risk, not the obvious general risks of an active war zone. Ukraine criminalises nothing about being trans; legal gender recognition exists (medicalised — a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol), and a resilient civil society (Gender Stream, Insight) operates openly. Kyiv hosted a three-day Trans Forum in June 2026 even during the war.

Trans-specific frictions exist but mostly affect residents, not visitors: trans women with male passports cannot leave the country under martial law (conscription), and wartime document checks can out people. A foreign visitor's passport is not subject to mobilisation rules, so border crossing is governed by standard wartime entry rules. There is no SOGI-specific hate-crime law, societal attitudes lag EU averages, and the healthcare system is war-disrupted (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption reported).

Ukraine scores far above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) — no criminalisation, no state persecution, functioning NGOs — and below Serbia (0.64) and Moldova (0.65), reflecting wartime institutional strain and weaker legal protections rather than active hostility.
records.current_localsOnly: The medicalised LGR protocol, the martial-law exit ban on trans women with male passports, and the war-disrupted healthcare (hormone shortages) are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: General war risks (missile strikes, infrastructure, mobilisation) apply to all travelers and are out of scope for the trans-specific score. Trans residents' draft exposure is noted as context but does not govern the visitor score.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch essay (15 May 2024) 'When Laws Fail to Protect Trans People': Ukraine-trans war-displacement case work — cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating Military Medical Commission confirmation; a Ukrainian activist notes commission hours (8am-8pm) and gatekeeping ('if a doctor says I'm a woman, the state can shrug').
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (June 2022) covers Ukraine's trans community caught in the crosshairs of war.

ZMINA (28 Jul 2026): trans women in Ukraine now find it harder to obtain a diagnosis — stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers; Trans Forum 2026 (Kyiv, early June 2026) discussed the new draft Civil Code's effect on transition procedure and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation — visitor-relevant documentary friction for trans Ukrainians and those crossing borders.

Gender Stream (Ukrainian NGO): consultations and support — advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families evacuating from frontline regions to western Ukraine/EU, and helps with processing/reissuing documents for transgender people, including those planning to legally cross the border; documents that since martial law, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service.

European Parliament written question E-002018/2022 (Jun 2022): on the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, in the context of Parliament's resolution on war's impact on women.

Amnesty International (16 May 2013) report 'Nothing to Report': Ukraine's government must legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on a sexual-orientation/gender-identity basis amid a pervasive climate of homophobia; lawmakers urged to vote down proposals to criminalise; attacks routinely used as pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and peaceful public events.

Erasing 76 Crimes (30 Aug 2016): among three-country advances, a Ukrainian court ordered changes requested by two trans people to their passports and all other documents WITHOUT requiring sterilisation — a concrete legal-gain data point for document amendment.

Human Rights Watch (26 Jun 2012): LGBT activist Taras Karasiichuk was attacked near his Kyiv apartment — the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; diagnosed concussion and broken jaw, police did not immediately respond despite medical referral; HRW urged investigation into homophobic motive.

records.name: Moldova
records.current_summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected of the former-Soviet states outside the Baltics. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity, and Chisinau Pride marches through the city centre under police protection. Moldova is on the EU accession path, driving continued legal alignment.

Counterweights: there is still no accessible legal gender recognition (a medicalised process exists on paper but Genderdoc-M reports it is not functional in practice), the Orthodox Church and major politicians (including Chisinau's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements, and the breakaway Russian-controlled region of Transnistria has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat Transnistria as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.
records.current_outOfScope: Transnistria is scored as part of Moldova de jure but travelers should treat it separately: Russian-controlled, anti-LGBT propaganda law, no consular access. General poverty and corruption affect all travelers.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Moldova: a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the Equality Council confirmed discrimination, recommending preventive measures; hate speech remained serious with no meaningful state response (echoed in the European Commission country report); election-period political hate speech rose.

Amnesty International Moldova 2025: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted (impunity for past violations); in Russian-occupied Transnistria new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".

GENDERDOC-M report (2023) citing the Equality Council study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022" (published January 2023): acceptance of LGBT+ people is extremely low — 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues (social-distance 5.7), and marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022.

Attitude (2 February 2026) revisiting Moldova Pride 2024: participants of all ages and backgrounds joined the festivities — a country "slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity"; public Pride proceeds openly.

ECOM legislative analysis on SOGI and HIV in Moldova (Tallinn, 2024): identifies legal barriers affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV — access to justice, hate-crime and discrimination provisions — based on a survey of local partners, benchmarked against international standards.

PinkNews (19 May 2018): police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters trying to disrupt the annual Moldova Pride solidarity march in Chisinau (19 May) as marchers carried foam hearts; activists feared a repeat of earlier violent scenes.

PinkNews (1 March 2013): the Balti Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February that the northern city’s "gay propaganda" ban was unconstitutional and violated human rights — local church-led bans struck down after protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.

records.name: Luxembourg
records.current_summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — one of Europe's strongest trans jurisdictions. Legal gender recognition by self-determination since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018), with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body (CET) handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (Schengen), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression/sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law.
records.current_localsOnly: The self-determination LGR process (notably open to foreign nationals) is resident-facing administrative law.

sources.claim: Official Luxembourg government portal (Guichet.lu) page on applying to change one's gender status and first name(s) in the civil register - the administrative procedure for legal gender recognition.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): marriage and adoption; self-determination-based gender markers (no nonbinary markers); discrimination banned on sexual orientation and gender identity but not gender expression or sex characteristics; no measures on conversion practices or intersex interventions; in July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, criticised by organisations for missing depathologisation and other key elements.

Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale UPR submission (April 2023) for Luxembourg: describes the organisation's services and Luxembourg's equality laws (employment, goods and services, education, health), the CET equality body and the national LGBTI action plan.

Asher Fergusson's LGBTQ+ Travel Safety Index (updated June 2023): 400+ hours of research ranking all countries' laws for LGBTQ+ traveller safety, with a companion Global Transgender Rights Index - comparative data source covering Luxembourg.

Le Quotidien (June 2019, in French): 'Agressions LGBTphobes: un durcissement des sanctions attendu' - Luxembourg law lacks LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances; victims under-report; the justice minister signalled the law would evolve after ECRI's 2017 intervention.

Le Quotidien (May 2017, in French): Justice Minister Félix Braz presented a bill allowing trans and intersex people to change civil-status gender by declaration - replacing the long, costly judicial procedure; welcomed by associations.

Le Quotidien headline (July 2018) confirms the Chamber approved simplified civil-status change for trans people; body paywalled in fetched copy — vote split and procedure details unverifiable from the page itself.

records.name: Monaco
records.current_summary:
Monaco is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. There is no functioning legal gender recognition process (ILGA-Europe lists Monaco among states without one), but that is a resident-facing gap: a visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever. Monaco is a tiny, heavily-policed, very low-crime tourist enclave embedded in France; street violence of any kind is rare.

No bathroom laws, no border friction (entry via France, Schengen rules), no documented anti-trans incidents. The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness (no LGR, limited explicit trans protections). Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
records.current_localsOnly: The absence of any LGR process is resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: Family-law gaps (no marriage equality, cohabitation contracts only) are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

records.name: San Marino
records.current_summary:
San Marino is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. ILGA-Europe lists San Marino among states with no functioning legal gender recognition process (resident-facing gap only). There is no criminalisation, no bathroom law, no border friction (open border with Italy), and no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in this tiny, tourism-dependent republic surrounded by Italy.

The score reflects very high de facto safety combined with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, Legal gender recognition category (2026 edition): San Marino is listed among the countries where there is NO functioning legal or administrative process for legal gender recognition.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 - Legal Gender Recognition chapter: country-by-country findings for 2025, including Albania's rejection of a self-ID recommendation at UPR, trans activist Luana Myrto's legal action in Albania, Andorra's delayed hormone-treatment decree, and other European developments.

ILGA compilation of SOGIESC recommendations from the 34th UPR Working Group session (Nov 2019) - includes San Marino's review among 12 countries examined; documents the SOGIESC recommendations each state received and accepted.
Euronews (4 Jun 2019): citizens voted by referendum to insert a clause prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation into the constitution of San Marino — the motion passed.

The Guardian (4 Apr 2022): Paolo Rondelli appointed captain regent — the world's first openly gay head of state (six-month term, no executive power); the article notes homosexuality was punishable by jail time in San Marino until 2004 and legal recognition of gay couples followed in 2016.
Euronews Italia (16 Nov 2018): San Marino's legislature approved a civil-unions law, described as 'leaner than the Cirinnà' Italian statute — the relationship-recognition framework in force.

records.name: Liechtenstein
records.current_summary:
Liechtenstein is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned, but gender identity, gender expression, and sex characteristics are not included in any anti-discrimination legislation, and there is no legal gender recognition law. These are resident-facing gaps: a visitor faces no legal exposure.

Liechtenstein is a very small, very low-crime Alpine country closely integrated with Switzerland; there is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence, no bathroom law, and no border friction (Schengen via Switzerland/Austria). Social attitudes are conservative but not mobilised-hostile. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
records.current_localsOnly: No LGR law and no gender-identity anti-discrimination coverage — resident-facing gaps.
records.current_outOfScope: Anti-discrimination and LGR gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): mixed situation - same-sex relations legal and sexual-orientation discrimination banned, but gender identity/expression/sex characteristics not covered by any anti-discrimination law; no legal gender marker change; IGM not prohibited; marriage and joint adoption available since January 2025; the state religion is Roman Catholicism and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality; first Pride in 2022.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers tiny European states (including Liechtenstein) playing catch-up on LGBT equality.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Liechtenstein' (March 2012): with a population of ~35,000 there is no organised gay scene - friendship networks are the scene; 'few organized enemies... no religious extremists, no right-wing skinheads, no political rogues demanding homophobic laws'; gay people live comfortably with little interference.

360° magazine (Jan 2016, in French): Prince Hans-Adam II called rainbow families 'irresponsible' in his New Year interview, said children have 'a right to a normal family', and suggested Liechtenstein could 'ignore' an adverse European Court of Human Rights ruling; local LGBT organisation Flay said it was 'choqué'; the Freie Liste called the remarks contrary to the Constitution and the ECHR.

Landtag motion (Sept 2022, in German): 'Motion zur Öffnung der Ehe für alle' - MPs' motion to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation, removing all remaining legal differences; notes registered partnerships are seen as a 'second-class marriage' and that the Prince had said in 2021 he had nothing against marriage equality except adoption.

records.name: Vatican City
records.current_summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — and an unusual case: it is a 0.49 km² tourist enclave (museums, basilica, square) with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathrooms inspections, no morality police, and the Swiss Guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile: the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and there is obviously no legal recognition or protection of any kind. But this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism — the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone). Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
records.current_outOfScope: Doctrinal positions are climate signals; Vatican employment and canon-law matters are resident-facing.

sources.claim: PinkNews (2 Oct 2008): Catholic officials rejected France's first-choice candidate as ambassador to the Holy See because he is gay, forcing Paris to name a different envoy -- documented instance of the Vatican government refusing an LGBT person in diplomatic relations.

Vatican Congregation for Catholic Education (2019): 'Male and Female He Created Them - Towards a Path of Dialogue on the Question of Gender Theory in Education' - the Vatican's educational document opposing 'gender theory', which it says 'denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman' and 'eliminat[es] the anthropological basis of the family'.

sources.title: Fiducia Supplicans (Wikipedia)
sources.claim: Overview of Fiducia Supplicans: DDF declaration under Pope Francis (issued 20 Mar 2023) permitting spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage; a January 2024 DDF press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves -- the current Holy See posture on blessing gay couples (fetched, document coverage verified).

sources.title: LGBT rights in Vatican City (Wikipedia)
sources.claim: Overview: no documented modern criminal-law persecution of consensual homosexual conduct in Vatican City itself (decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots); the Holy See's institutional posture against homosexuality and gender theory drives policy -- legal baseline distinguishing the Church's diplomacy from the city-state's own law (fetched, article text verified).
